Cannabis Label Versioning Workflow for Multi-State Brands

A cannabis label versioning workflow produces state-specific labels from one master template by moving state-variable fields in as print data.

If you hold licenses in five states, you do not have five compliance problems. You have a production-control problem. This guide is for cannabis operations, packaging, and compliance leads who own artwork release and press scheduling, and it covers the master-template structure, the variable-data field map, the run-grouping method, and the version-level QC checklist.

Requirements vary by state and change frequently. Verify current rules with your regulator or compliance counsel before releasing any artwork. What follows is the operational system that sits underneath those rules.

A cannabis label versioning workflow is a controlled process for producing state-specific label versions from one master template. Brand and structural elements stay locked, while state-variable fields (warning content, potency format, license number, and the track-and-trace zone) move as data through variable data printing, then get verified and traced to each batch. It controls four things: one governed master template per product family and die, a state-version data table owned by compliance, a variable-data merge that carries batch and track-and-trace values, and a QC gate that proves the right version printed before rolls leave production. Arrow Systems’ ArrowJet Aqua 330R is the water-based digital inkjet label press that supports this workflow. A governed workflow reduces operational risk; it does not replace compliance review.

Key Takeaways

  • Treat multi-state labeling as a production-control problem: product count multiplied by license count makes the artwork file library grow faster than the business.
  • Use one master template per product family and die, with locked brand zones and controlled variable zones that each have a character limit, a minimum type size, and a defined overflow behavior.
  • Keep state content in a state-version data table owned by compliance, and merge it with batch-level data (lot, test date, UID) so one print pass produces the correct version and the correct lot data.
  • Group runs by substrate and finishing first, then die, then state version, so low-volume states share one setup instead of triggering separate minimums.
  • Verify every version with its own proof, a first article at each version transition, scanned barcodes and UIDs, labeled rolls, and a retained print record.
  • A new die, substrate, structural layout, or finishing spec is a new base template and usually a new run. A change inside the existing frames is a data record.

Why State-by-State Cannabis Versioning Is an Operational Problem, Not Just a Compliance Problem

Each state multiplies label SKUs, artwork files, minimum orders, and obsolete inventory, which makes versioning a production-control problem.

The regulatory text is the input. The cost sits downstream of it: a file library that duplicates every product for every market, flexo minimums that force you to buy more labels than a state version will consume, short changeovers that burn setup time and substrate, and inventory that becomes scrap the moment a state updates its packaging and labeling rules.

How one product becomes many label SKUs

A single 100mg gummy pouch can generate a dozen label SKUs without a formulation change. Multiply your product count by your license count, and the label file library grows faster than the business does. The variables that typically differ by market are listed below.

Warning symbol or icon

The required warning symbol or icon and its placement differ by state.

Warning text block

The mandated warning text and its content differ by state.

Potency declaration format

Format differences include per serving versus per package, THC/CBD ordering, units, and rounding conventions.

Licensee identification and license number

Licensee name and license number fields vary by license and by market.

Track-and-trace or UID zone

Zone dimensions and encoding differ by market.

Serving-size, dosage, and testing statements

Required statements and their wording differ by state.

Language, font-size, and contrast requirements

Type size, contrast, and language rules differ by market.

Where the cost actually lands

Most teams underestimate how much of the expense sits outside the label itself.

Duplicated artwork

When each state version is its own file, a brand refresh or a potency format update means dozens of files to re-edit, route for approval, and reorder.

Minimum order quantities

Conventional flexo economics push you to buy quantities a low-volume state version will not consume before the next rule revision.

Storage and obsolescence

Rolls sit in racks tied to one destination market, and a packaging rule update turns them into scrap.

Changeover drag

High-mix, short-run label production repeats plates, dies, and setup for every version.

The risk view

The operational failure mode is applying the wrong state version to product destined for another market. That can lead to quarantine, relabeling, schedule disruption, and a reportable compliance event. A governed versioning workflow reduces operational risk; it does not eliminate regulatory risk and does not replace compliance review.

Setting Up a Master Template System for State Versions

Use one master template per product family, with locked brand zones and controlled variable zones populated from a state-version data record

Fixed zones vs. controlled variable zones

Zone category

Fields

How it changes

Fixed zones

Brand mark, logo lockup, and color system; product name and flavor/strain descriptor position; structural die line, bleed, and safe-area boundaries; net weight and net contents placement; brand copy, web address, and social handles

Only through a formal artwork revision owned by brand

Controlled variable zones

State warning symbol or icon frame; state warning text block (fixed frame, variable content); potency/THC-CBD declaration panel and its format; licensee name and license number field; serving, dosage, and testing statements; track-and-trace / UID area (symbol type, size, quiet zone); batch/lot number, test date, packaged-on or expiration date

Populated per state version from a data record

The discipline lives in the frame, not the content. Each variable zone gets a maximum character count, a minimum type size, and a defined overflow behavior, so a longer state warning block cannot push into brand artwork or the die line.

Naming conventions and version locking

Pick a naming scheme a production planner can read at a glance and that sorts correctly in a file browser, for example PRODUCTFAMILY_SIZE_DIE_STATE_TEMPLATEVERSION_DATE. These rules are worth enforcing:

  • Keep one source-of-truth master per product family and die, with no local copies.
  • Use semantic versioning, where a structural change bumps the major version and a text-block change bumps the minor version.
  • Lock the layers for fixed zones, and limit edit permissions to the artwork owner.
  • Record a revision log entry for every state version change, including approver and date.
  • Archive superseded versions out of the active print directory instead of deleting them.

Ownership and approval gates

Ambiguous ownership is where wrong versions come from, so each zone gets an owner.

Owner

Owns

Approval role

Brand/marketing

Fixed zones

Approves any change that touches fixed zones

Compliance

State-variable content: warning text, potency format, required statements

Signs off on each state record before it enters the print-ready library

Production/packaging

Die line, substrate, finishing spec, and the data mapping between the state table and the template

Closes the production gate for each state record

No state version becomes print-eligible until all three gates are closed for that record.

Building for the next license, not just current states

Design the template to absorb a new market without a rebuild. Size the warning block frame for the most demanding content you have encountered, and reserve a UID zone even in states that do not require one. Keep the potency panel modular so a different declaration format becomes a data swap rather than a layout redesign.

Variable Data Printing: What Gets Swapped Per State and What Stays Fixed

State-level and batch-level fields move as data in variable data label printing; die, substrate, layout, and finishing changes need a new template.

Data-driven fields

In a well-built variable data printing (VDP) setup for cannabis labels, these fields typically move as data.

Data layer

Fields

Maintained in

State-version record

State warning text strings and the associated symbol asset reference; potency declaration values and the format template that renders them; license number and licensee name; serving and testing statement blocks

State-version data table

Batch-level record

Barcode, QR, and UID payloads; batch/lot, test date, and package date

Batch data table

What requires a new base template

Variable data has practical limits. Plan for a separate template, and usually a separate run, when you change any of the items below.

Change

Why it needs a new template or run

Die shape or label size

A different cut means different tooling and a different press setup.

Substrate or adhesive

Facestock, liner, and adhesive changes affect feed, ink interaction, and finishing.

Structural layout

A booklet, extended-content, or wrap-around construction is a different product, not a version.

Finishing spec

Lamination, varnish, and cold foil differences generally group separately. Downstream options are covered in Arrow’s label finishing systems.

The rule of thumb: if it changes what the press and finisher are physically doing, it is a new run. If it only changes what renders inside the existing frames, it is a data record.

Mapping a state-version data table to template fields

Maintain a single state-version table (a spreadsheet, CSV export, or database view) where each row is one state version and each column maps to a named template field. Add a second table, or extend the same one, for batch-level data: lot number, test date, and UID string. A practical mapping approach follows.

  1. Name every variable field in the template exactly as its column header in the data source.
  2. Validate the file before submission: character counts, required-field completeness, and barcode payload format.
  3. Merge state-level and batch-level records so one pass produces the correct state version and the correct lot data.
  4. Version the data file alongside the template so the print record reflects both.

Where operations automation fits

This is the point where labeling stops being a procurement task. When the state-version table, ERP item master, production schedule, and seed to sale system feed the print job, automation removes the manual re-keying that produces most version errors. Integration depth varies by platform, so scope connectivity (file formats, network access, API availability) during system evaluation rather than after.

Scheduling State-Specific Runs Without Wasting Substrate or Setup Time

Group jobs by substrate and finishing, then die, then state version, so low-volume states share one setup instead of separate minimums.

Group by substrate and die first, then sequence versions

Build the schedule in this order every time.

  1. Substrate and finishing. All jobs on the same facestock and lamination spec group together.
  2. Die and label size. Within substrate, group by tooling to avoid changeovers.
  3. State version sequence. Inside that group, order versions as data records; the press does not stop between them.
  4. Batch data merge. Apply lot, test date, and UID at the record level within each version.

Consolidating low-volume states

Low-volume markets are where minimum-order economics hurt most. If three states share a substrate and die, they belong in one scheduled run, not three procurement events with three minimums and three sets of leftovers.

The following is an illustrative example, not a performance claim or a quote. A brand produces a 1 oz flower jar label on one substrate and one die across four markets. Weekly demand might run 4,000 for the largest market and 600 to 900 for each of the other three.

Print close to use

Track and trace, batch, and test-date data frequently arrive late in the schedule. Printing closer to fill removes the guesswork: labels are produced once the batch data exists, aligned to the fill sequence, and staged by destination market instead of held as speculative inventory.

QC: How to Verify the Right Version Printed Before Labels Leave Production

Prove the right version printed with per-version proofs, first articles, scanned codes, labeled rolls, and a retained print record.

Pre-run proof and first-article sign-off per version

Every version in a grouped run gets its own proof, not one proof for the whole run. Compliance approves the state-variable content, and production approves placement, legibility, and die registration. When the run starts, pull a first article at each version transition and sign off before the segment continues.

Barcode, UID, and data-integrity checks

Scan, do not eyeball. Confirm that the barcode or UID decodes to the expected payload, that the decoded value matches the batch record, and that grade and quiet-zone requirements are met. Spot-check data integrity at the start, middle, and end of each version segment to catch mid-run data drift.

Roll identification and segregation

Every finished roll should carry a physical or printed identifier showing product, template version, state version, batch, quantity, and destination market. Segregate staged rolls by destination so a filling line cannot pick the wrong version without breaking a rule.

Retained print record

Keep a print record with the batch file: template version, data file version, state version, quantity printed, quantity scrapped, roll IDs, approvals, and scan verification results. That record answers “which version and which data printed on this lot?” months later without reconstructing it from memory.

Operator checklist

  1. Confirm the work order state version list matches the loaded data file.
  2. Verify substrate, die, and finishing spec against the job ticket.
  3. Check that an approved proof is present and signed for each version in the run.
  4. Pull a first article and sign it at every version transition.
  5. Scan the barcode/UID and match the decoded value to the batch record.
  6. Spot-check variable fields for truncation, overflow, and blank values.
  7. Apply a roll ID with state version and destination market.
  8. Complete the print record and file it with the batch documentation.

Short-run economics across many SKUs

Fit considerations

Configuration depends on your substrate and adhesive set, die and label geometry, finishing requirements (lamination, varnish, slitting, rewind), and how label data connects to your ERP, scheduling, and seed-to-sale systems. Frequently Asked Questions — Cannabis Label Versioning for Multi-State Brands

Common questions from cannabis operations, packaging, and compliance teams building a state-by-state label versioning workflow.

Do we need a separate label file for every state we ship into?

No, and separate files are usually the root of the problem. A better structure is one governed master template per product family and die, with state-specific content held as records in a state-version data table. Brand and structural zones stay locked, while state warning content, potency format, license fields, and UID zones populate from data. You still need a separate base template when die shape, substrate, or structural layout changes. This collapses a large per-state file library into a small set of masters plus a maintainable data source.

Can batch, test date, and track-and-trace data print in the same pass as state-specific warning content?

Yes. In a variable data workflow, version-level fields and record-level fields merge into the same template at print time, so one pass can produce the correct state warning block along with the correct lot, test date, and UID. This matters because track-and-trace and testing data often arrive late in the schedule. Printing close to fill, with both data layers merged, avoids holding pre-printed inventory while you wait for batch information and avoids a second application step.

How do we keep state specific labels current when packaging rules change?

Treat the state version data table as a controlled document with a named compliance owner, a review cadence, and a change log. When a market updates its requirements, you edit one record instead of re-issuing dozens of artwork files, then route it through the compliance and production approval gates before it becomes print-eligible. Because production is print-to-demand, exposure to obsolete pre-printed inventory is lower. Requirements vary by state and change frequently, so confirm current rules with your regulator or compliance counsel before releasing updated artwork.

Which label fields typically change from one state version to the next?

The fields that typically differ by market are the warning symbol and its placement, the warning text block, the potency declaration format, licensee and license number fields, the track-and-trace or UID zone, serving-size, dosage, and testing statements, and language, font-size, and contrast requirements. In a governed workflow these live in a state-version data table rather than in separate artwork files.

When does a state version need a new base template instead of a data record?

A new base template, and usually a separate run, is needed when die shape or label size, substrate or adhesive, structural layout, or finishing spec changes. If the change only alters what renders inside the existing frames, it is a data record. If it changes what the press and finisher are physically doing, it is a new run.

Table of Contents

Water-Based vs UV-Cured Label Adhesive: Food & Pharma Guide

Water-based adhesives suit dry, ambient containers; UV-cured hot melts suit cold, wet, curved plastics. Neither is inherently food safe.

Water-based (aqueous acrylic) label adhesives dry from an emulsion, build adhesion over hours, and suit ambient, dry, high-surface-energy containers such as glass, PET, and cartons. UV-cured hot melt adhesives are 100% solids systems that crosslink under UV energy, giving higher shear strength, a wider temperature range, and stronger grip on cold, wet, curved, and low-surface-energy plastics such as HDPE and polypropylene. Neither chemistry is inherently food safe or pharma compliant: migration and compliance depend on the full label construction (adhesive, facestock, ink, and container) and its documented use. The right choice follows service conditions, not unit price.

Key Takeaways

  • Specify to worst-case service conditions, not typical ones: the hottest fill, the coldest storage, the wettest bottle, and the most aggressive product.
  • Treat migration as a construction question: the adhesive, facestock, ink, and container together determine risk, not the adhesive chemistry alone.
  • Demand a regulatory compliance statement and a written change-notification commitment from the supplier before sampling any label stock.
  • Prove performance with a condensation soak, a cold-room hold, and a full-speed line trial on your actual container and applicator.
  • Lock facestock, adhesive, liner, and print method as one specification under change control so no component is substituted silently.

Why Label Adhesive Choice Comes Down to Service Conditions

Adhesive failures in food, beverage, and pharma labeling come from cold, condensation, and curvature, not from the printing step.

This guide is written for packaging engineers, quality, and regulatory teams in food, beverage, nutraceutical, and pharmaceutical operations that specify self adhesive labels, also called pressure sensitive labels. The failure patterns are familiar. A juice bottle labeled at 38°F in a condensation-heavy zone lifts a quarter inch in the retail cooler. Bottle label adhesive is judged there, not on the line. A 2 mL vial at -20°C curls at the corners and pulls the barcode out of scanner range.

Neither failure is a printing problem, and both are what push teams to compare water based vs UV cured label adhesive in the first place. You will leave with how each chemistry is built, where migration risk originates, the documentation to demand from suppliers, and a five-step workflow for choosing the right adhesive for labels and locking a defensible label stock specification.

How Water-Based and UV-Cured Label Adhesives Are Formulated

Water-based adhesives dry from an acrylic emulsion; UV-curable hot melts are 100% solids that crosslink under UV energy after hot application.

Both chemistries serve as the adhesive layer in pressure sensitive adhesive labels, so the choice is made at the construction level, together with the facestock and liner.

Water-Based (Aqueous) Label Adhesives

Water-based adhesive structure

Water-based pressure sensitive adhesives, also called aqueous or emulsion adhesives, start as acrylic polymer particles dispersed in water. The dispersion is coated onto a liner or facestock, then driven through a drying oven. The water evaporates and the polymer particles coalesce into a continuous tacky film.

What stays in the dried film

The dried film contains the acrylic polymer plus whatever was formulated in: surfactants that stabilize the emulsion, tackifying resins that boost initial grab, and sometimes crosslinkers that raise shear strength. Surfactants come up most often in migration discussions because they are relatively low in molecular weight and mobile.

In-service behavior

Aqueous acrylics behave predictably. Clarity is typically good, UV and aging resistance are strong, and adhesion builds over hours rather than instantly. The tradeoff is moisture sensitivity, both during coating and in service. On a wet or condensation-covered container, water at the bond line interferes with wet-out and the label never develops full adhesion.

Typical food and nutraceutical uses

Aqueous chemistry is the default for a large share of adhesive food labels and nutraceutical labeling: dry goods cartons, supplement bottles stored at room temperature, ambient glass and PET, and paper facestock work where cost per square inch and documentation familiarity both favor an established construction.

UV-Cured Hot Melt Label Adhesives

UV-curable hot melt structure

UV-curable hot melt adhesives are 100% solids systems, with no water and no solvent carrier. They are applied hot as a molten film and then exposed to UV energy. Photoinitiators absorb that energy and trigger crosslinking of the polymer backbone, converting a soft hot melt into a network structure.

Performance advantage of crosslinking

The crosslinked network delivers higher shear strength, better resistance to cold flow and oozing, and a wider usable temperature range at both ends. That is why UV-curable constructions are typically specified for high temperature adhesive labels on hot-fill and pasteurized products. UV-curable systems also tend to grab aggressively on low-surface-energy plastics such as HDPE and polypropylene, and they resist the peel forces generated when a label wraps a small-diameter vial or ampoule.

Cure completeness as the controlling variable

Under-cured adhesive retains unreacted oligomers and residual photoinitiator — exactly the low-molecular-weight species that migration and extractables reviews focus on. Photoinitiator selection, lamp output, and line speed during coating therefore carry compliance implications, not just performance ones. Cure control is a converting process question, and it belongs in supplier qualification.

Where UV-curable chemistry earns its premium

UV-curable chemistry earns its premium in beverage cold chain, chilled and frozen foods, squeezable HDPE containers, and pharmaceutical primary containers where labels must survive autoclave cycles, cryogenic storage, or repeated isopropyl wipe-down. Freezer adhesive labels in particular have to hold through condensation and deep cold, which is where aqueous grades not formulated for cold application tend to flag.

Food Safety: Where Migration Risk Actually Comes From

Migration is a property of the whole label construction, not the adhesive alone; both chemistries can be compliant or non-compliant.

Direct answer: Migration is a system property, not an adhesive property. Risk depends on the adhesive layer, the barrier performance of the facestock, whether contact is direct or indirect, and the application and service conditions. Both aqueous and UV-curable constructions can be compliant or non-compliant depending on build and use.

Most pressure sensitive labels on food packaging are an indirect food contact application. The adhesive sits on the outside of a container wall or carton, and the container itself is the barrier. The working question is whether the facestock, ink, and container together block migration of adhesive components into the food.

The functional barrier concept is central. A metallized or polymer film facestock on a glass bottle presents a very different migration pathway than porous uncoated paper applied to a thin-wall squeezable pouch. Set-off during roll storage and diffusion through low-barrier substrates are both plausible routes, and neither depends on which chemistry you picked.

Application and Product Conditions That Raise or Lower Risk

Fatty and oily products

Fats are aggressive extractants for many adhesive components, so fatty and oily products raise migration risk.

Hot-fill and pasteurization

Elevated temperature during hot-fill and pasteurization accelerates diffusion of adhesive components.

Acidic products

Acidic products such as juice, sauces, and kombucha belong in the migration risk map.

Thin-wall and flexible packaging

Squeezable bottles, pouches, and films have limited barrier, so the container offers less protection against migration.

Porous or uncoated substrates

Paperboard sleeves and kraft wraps are porous, which gives adhesive components an easier path through the substrate.

Long shelf life

Migration accumulates over time, so a longer shelf life increases exposure.

Regulatory Frameworks for Food Contact Adhesives

U.S. frameworks

The U.S. indirect food additive provisions for adhesives in 21 CFR Part 175 and FDA’s food contact substance notification program describe how adhesive components used in food packaging are evaluated.

EU frameworks for exported SKUs

Exported SKUs may also be assessed against EU Regulation 1935/2004 and, where plastics are involved, Regulation 10/2011.

Why no adhesive is “FDA approved” on its own

These frameworks evaluate substances within a defined use, which is why no adhesive can be meaningfully described as “FDA approved” as a standalone material.

How to read supplier compliance statements

A supplier statement typically confirms that a formulation’s components are addressed under named regulations for a described use condition. It is not a blanket clearance, and it does not transfer responsibility for the finished package. That determination stays with the brand owner or manufacturer, informed by supplier documentation.

Pharmaceutical Compliance: Change Control Is the Real Constraint

In GMP operations, label adhesive sits inside a controlled specification, so any change goes through GMP change control, not purchasing.

Why adhesive is a controlled component

In a GMP environment, the technical comparison is only half the work. Pressure sensitive label stock is a specified component, and expectations under 21 CFR Parts 210 and 211 mean the adhesive generally sits inside a controlled specification. It is not an interchangeable commodity a converter can substitute mid-year, which makes an adhesive swap a GMP change control event rather than a purchasing decision.

What an adhesive change can trigger

Under a documented GMP change control process, an adhesive change may trigger specification revision, supplier qualification activity, retention sample updates, stability or transport assessment, and potentially requalification of the labeling operation. Change control in GMP settings expects the change, its risk assessment, and its approval to be documented before the new stock is used. Teams that treat an adhesive swap as a purchasing decision usually discover the documentation cost afterward.

Extractables and leachables on primary containers

When the label sits on a primary container — a vial, ampoule, prefilled syringe, or blister card — extractables and leachables thinking extends to the label construction. The questions are whether adhesive components can migrate through the container wall or closure system, and whether the facestock and ink contribute to the extractables profile. Extractables are what a material can release under aggressive laboratory conditions; leachables are what actually migrates into the product in normal storage and use.

Lifecycle conditions adhesion must survive

Adhesion has to hold across terminal sterilization or autoclave cycles, 2–8°C cold chain with repeated condensation events, -80°C or liquid nitrogen storage, small-diameter curved surfaces, and isopropyl or quaternary disinfectant wipe-down in clinical settings.

Serialization and scanning requirements

Serialization and unit-dose formats add a scanning requirement, so legibility and flatness matter as much as bond strength.

Documentation to Request Before You Approve a Label Stock

  • Request a technical data sheet that states the service temperature range and the minimum application temperature.
  • Request a regulatory compliance statement that names the frameworks and use conditions evaluated.
  • Request a statement of composition or component disclosure where the supplier will provide it.
  • Request lot traceability from the adhesive coater through converting.
  • Request a written change-notification commitment covering formulation, coater, and raw material source changes.
  • Request cure process control information for UV-curable constructions.

How to Specify the Right Adhesive for Your Label Stock

Specify label adhesive in five steps: worst case, condition matrix, documentation, bench and line trials, then a locked construction.

Step 1: Define the worst-case contact and service scenario

Use the worst case, not the typical case: the hottest fill, the coldest storage, the wettest bottle, the most aggressive product. Work one SKU family at a time.

Step 2: Build a condition matrix

For each SKU group, document container material and surface energy, container surface temperature at application, moisture or condensation at application, service temperature range and duration, chemical exposure (product contact, disinfectants, ice slurry), required shelf life, contact classification, and end-of-life recyclability requirements. This matrix is what a converter or adhesive supplier needs before recommending a construction.

Step 3: Request documentation before sampling

Use the supplier documentation checklist above. If a supplier cannot produce a regulatory compliance statement or a change-notification commitment, that is a finding, not a delay.

Step 4: Run bench and line trials

At minimum: 24-hour and 7-day peel on the actual container, cold-room hold at your storage temperature, condensation soak with labels applied to chilled containers, isopropyl wipe-down and abrasion checks, and a full-speed line trial through your applicator with observation of matrix strip and any adhesive ooze. Hold samples for the product shelf life where feasible.

Step 5: Lock the specification under change control

Record facestock, adhesive, liner, and print method together as one construction. Adhesive performance depends on the whole laminate, so approving components separately invites a silent substitution later.

Where Digital Printing and Finishing Fit in the Specification

Why digital production pushes constructions to converge

Adhesive and liner choices interact directly with your automation roadmap. On-demand digital label printing turns pressure sensitive label printing into a short-run, per-SKU process, so you can retire obsolete pre-printed inventory. For digital pressure sensitive labels for pharma and food alike, it also pushes your constructions to converge. High-changeover schedules reward a small set of validated constructions that cover clustered condition profiles rather than a unique stock per SKU.

The ink layer is part of the construction

The printed ink sits in the same stack as the adhesive, facestock, and liner, so it affects the migration picture too. The ArrowJet Aqua 330R prints with water-based pigment inks on a Memjet DuraFlex® engine and is Nestlé Guidance compliant, so food and beverage teams that print their own labels start from an ink set that meets that guidance. The finished construction still needs its own migration assessment, so test printed samples on your actual container and product.

Include finishing in the line trial

Matrix strip behavior and adhesive ooze onto die stations only show up on the finishing equipment you actually run, so include die-cutting and slitting in the line trial. For short-run, high-changeover production, pairing your digital press with Arrow’s label finishing systems lets you run that trial across the full print-and-finish path.

Decision Summary

Match adhesive to service conditions: water-based for ambient dry goods, UV-curable for cold, wet, curved, or demanding pharma containers.

Aqueous acrylic typically fits

Ambient-temperature glass and PET, dry goods and paperboard, supplement and nutraceutical bottles, clear-on-clear film labels where optical quality drives the spec, applications needing removability or clean release, and programs where an established, well-documented water based pressure sensitive adhesive construction lowers qualification effort.

UV-curable hot melt typically fits

A UV curable hot melt adhesive suits chilled and frozen beverage and food, HDPE and polypropylene containers, small-diameter vials and ampoules, labels exposed to disinfectant wipe-down, hot-fill and pasteurized products, and pharmaceutical primary containers with demanding thermal cycles.

Evaluate a different construction entirely when

One SKU must span both ambient application and deep-freeze service (consider a validated all-temperature adhesive), the container geometry defeats any flat label (consider shrink sleeve or in-mold labeling), the container is returnable or reusable with residue constraints, or recyclability targets call for a wash-off adhesive system.

Frequently Asked Questions — Water-Based vs UV-Cured Label Adhesive

Common questions from packaging, quality, and regulatory teams comparing label adhesive chemistries for food and pharmaceutical use.

Is water-based or UV-cured adhesive inherently safer for food contact?

No. Neither chemistry is inherently safer. Migration potential depends on the specific formulation, the barrier performance of the facestock and container, whether the application is direct or indirect food contact, and the product and service conditions. A well-documented aqueous acrylic under a film facestock on glass and a fully cured UV-curable adhesive can both be appropriate. An under-cured UV film or a heavily surfactant-loaded emulsion under porous paper on a fatty product can both raise legitimate concerns. Evaluate the construction in its intended use, supported by supplier documentation.

Does changing label adhesive chemistry trigger requalification in a GMP environment?

Usually some level of assessment, yes. Because label stock is generally a controlled component, an adhesive change is evaluated through your GMP change control procedure rather than handled as a purchasing substitution. Depending on risk, that can include specification revision, supplier qualification, updated compliance documentation, adhesion and legibility testing across storage and distribution conditions, extractables assessment for primary container labels, and retention sample updates. Scope the change-control impact before you approve samples. It often shifts the economics of a chemistry switch more than unit price does.

Which adhesive performs better on cold, wet bottles and freezer packs?

UV-curable hot melt constructions usually hold an advantage. Aqueous emulsions depend on wet-out at the bond line, and condensation plus a surface below the adhesive’s minimum application temperature both suppress bond formation. That combination is the common cause of flagging on chilled beverage bottles. Aqueous adhesives formulated specifically for cold and moist application do exist and perform well within their stated limits. Verify with a condensation soak trial and a cold-room hold on your actual container at line temperature rather than relying on the data sheet range.

What documentation should I request from a label adhesive supplier before approving a label stock?

Request six items: a technical data sheet with the service temperature range and minimum application temperature; a regulatory compliance statement naming the frameworks and use conditions evaluated; a statement of composition or component disclosure where the supplier will provide it; lot traceability from adhesive coater through converting; a written change-notification commitment covering formulation, coater, and raw material source changes; and cure process control information for UV-curable constructions. If a supplier cannot produce a compliance statement or a change-notification commitment, treat that as a finding, not a delay.

What is the difference between extractables and leachables for label adhesives?

Extractables are compounds that can be pulled out of a label material under aggressive laboratory conditions, such as strong solvents or heat. Leachables are the compounds that actually migrate into the product under normal storage and use. Extractables and leachables testing therefore usually starts with a worst-case extractables study and then confirms what appears in the product over its shelf life. For labels on primary containers, the scope is set by the drug product owner’s quality and regulatory team, supported by supplier documentation.

Food contact, extractables, and GMP compliance determinations are the responsibility of the brand owner or manufacturer and should be confirmed with qualified regulatory and quality professionals. Is Your Confectionery Brand Ready to Bring Flexible Packaging In-House?

In-house flexible packaging pays off for confectionery brands with many SKUs, short reorders, and frequent artwork changes, not high footage alone.

Bringing flexible packaging in-house makes sense for confectionery brands that run many SKUs, short reorder quantities, and frequent artwork revisions, not simply large total annual footage. Three triggers decide it: run length per purchase order, format and film-structure mix, and the landed cost of outsourced printed film, including minimum-order overage, obsolescence, and expedite premiums. Arrow Systems’ ArrowJet Aqua 800M is a wide-web water-based inkjet printer for digital flexible packaging, built for brands and co-manufacturers with that high-mix profile. A portfolio of a few long, stable SKUs on one or two film structures is usually better served by a converter.

Key Takeaways

  • Run length per purchase order, active SKU count, reorder frequency, and footage by film structure drive the in-house decision, while total annual footage is the least useful input.
  • Label press experience does not transfer to wide-web flexible pouch printing, because substrates, tension control, finishing chains, and QC scope all change.
  • Compare total landed cost, including minimum-order overage, obsolescence, expedite premiums, and missed seasonal windows, rather than the converter’s price per thousand.
  • Nine readiness items, from artwork version control to seal and barrier QA, must be in place before capital is committed, because in-house printing fails on process discipline more often than on equipment.
  • The ArrowJet Aqua 800M suits high-mix confectionery portfolios, and a small set of long-running core SKUs on stable film is better served by a converter.

When the In-House Question Comes Up for Confectionery Brands

The question usually surfaces after a converter’s minimum order or a label-press assumption, and neither moment is a decision on its own.

Digital printing on flexible packaging changes the economics for some confectionery portfolios and not for others. This guide is written for confectionery brand owners, co-manufacturers, and the ops, engineering, QA, and packaging leads who have to live with the decision, plus the executive who signs the capital request. It gives you three go/no-go triggers, a landed-cost worksheet you can fill in with your own invoices, and a nine-point readiness checklist before you evaluate any digital flexible packaging printer.

Moment one: the converter minimum order

A converter quotes a minimum order quantity (MOQ) that locks you into nine months of printed film for a Valentine’s gummy with a six-week selling window.

Moment two: the label-press assumption

Your team, already running a roll-label press in the plant, assumes stand-up pouches are the same job on a wider web.

Neither moment is a decision. Both are symptoms.

Roll Labels vs. Flexible Pouches: Why In-House Experience Does Not Transfer

Label press experience does not carry over to wide-web flexible packaging, because substrates, finishing chains, and failure modes all change.

Running a digital label printer does not qualify you to run a wide-web flexible packaging printer. The substrates behave differently, the finishing chain is longer, and the failure modes shift from cosmetic to functional. A bad label is ugly. A bad seal is a product loss.

Factor

Roll label in-house

Flexible pouch in-house

Web width

Narrow web, sized to label die layouts

Wide web sized to pouch layouts, gussets, and multiple lanes

Substrate

Unsupported films, laminates, and metallized barrier structures with stretch and static behavior

Ink and adhesion

Adhesion to coated PS stock; topcoat compatibility is well understood

Adhesion plus crease and flex resistance on treated films; surface energy and dyne level matter

Tension and registration

The liner carries the web, so tension is forgiving

Thin, stretchy film; tension control drives registration and repeat length

Downstream steps

Lamination to a sealant web, slitting, then pouch making or supply as rollstock to a filler

QC scope

All of that plus seal integrity, lamination bond, barrier performance, and print survival through forming and filling

Operator skill

Label press operation and finishing

Web handling on film, tension and lamination judgment, plus converting coordination

Two implications matter for candy brands.

Printing in-house does not mean pouch making in-house

Many brands produce printed rollstock internally and either keep converting with a pouch maker or feed film straight to a vertical form-fill-seal or flow-wrap line.

The QC plan has to grow

Seal and barrier verification is not a print function, and it needs a named owner.

Volume Trigger: What Run Length Justifies a Wide-Web Flexible Packaging Press

In-house digital flexible packaging printing pays off with many SKUs, short reorders, and frequent artwork revisions, not annual footage alone.

Total annual volume is the number finance reaches for first, and it is the least useful input. Four inputs actually drive the answer:

Run length per SKU per order

The quantity you would buy on one purchase order, not annual usage.

Active SKU count and churn

How many SKUs exist, and how many are new, seasonal, or retailer-specific each year.

Reorder frequency

Four small pulls a year per SKU behaves nothing like one large pull.

Annual linear footage by structure

Group footage by film structure, because each structure carries its own qualification work and its own minimum order.

Portfolio type

Typical profile

Likely answer

Favors in-house

Dozens of active SKUs, short runs in the hundreds to low thousands of pouches per order, seasonal waves around Halloween, winter holidays, Valentine’s Day, and Easter, frequent flavor tests, and regular net-weight, allergen, or promotional-flash revisions

Build the in-house business case

Stays outsourced

A handful of core SKUs running long, stable orders on one or two qualified structures, with artwork that changes once every few years

Keep the converter relationship

If a few SKUs carry most of your footage and rarely change, a converter will beat you on unit cost and you will not recover the capital. Say that out loud before you build the business case.

Work the Stranded-Film Arithmetic With Your Own Invoices

  1. For each seasonal SKU, take the converter minimum order for its structure and subtract the footage the season actually consumes.
  2. Multiply the stranded difference by your quoted film price per linear foot.
  3. Add the plate or cylinder charge for every artwork revision, because conventional flexographic printing needs plates and rotogravure needs engraved cylinders.
  4. Total the result across your seasonal and limited-edition SKUs.

Teams often find that figure larger than the price-per-foot concession they spent the whole quote cycle negotiating. For the sachet-format view of the same problem, see Arrow’s guide to the real cost of SKU proliferation in sachet packaging.

Format Trigger: When Your Candy Product Mix Needs Pouch Capability

Format variety, not volume, is what an in-house press solves when a portfolio spans several film structures and dozens of graphics.

Confectionery portfolios diverge hardest from the brands that flexible packaging economics were originally built around. Open your SKU sheet and count how many of these confectionery flexible packaging formats you actually run:

Stand-up pouches and gusseted pouches

Printed stand-up pouches and side-gusset formats for gummies, sour belts, and mixed bags, from share size through resealable family bags.

Flow-wrap film

Flow wrap packaging for bars, single-twist hard candy, and individually wrapped pieces.

Club multipacks and warehouse-channel variants

Different counts, net weights, and retailer marks on one recipe.

Private-label versions

A single base formulation, each version needing custom printed flexible packaging with its own artwork, brand-owner approval cycle, and revision schedule.

Seasonal graphics and limited editions

Tied to a retail window that closes whether your film arrived or not.

Flavor-test runs

A few hundred units for sampling, e-commerce, or one account.

Substrate Requirements by Candy Type

Gummies

Gummies push toward moisture and oxygen barrier and need a sealant that survives sugar dust and oil in the seal area.

Chocolate

Chocolate is heat- and light-sensitive and sits in a different structure conversation entirely.

Hard candy

Hard candy is unforgiving about moisture ingress.

Every structure change restarts qualification, which is exactly why a converter-managed portfolio with many structures feels slow. If your formats and structures are few and stable, format variety is not your trigger. If you are managing several structures across dozens of graphics and multiple pouch styles, format churn, not volume, is what an in-house press solves.

Cost Trigger: Landed Cost of Outsourced Film vs. In-House Printing

Compare total landed cost, not price per thousand, because the lines a converter quote leaves out are usually where the money sits.

Build this worksheet from your own finance and procurement data, covering one year, with actuals wherever possible:

How to Read the Worksheet

Together they often outweigh the price-per-foot gap under negotiation.

These are the hardest lines to source and frequently the largest.

Qualification scrap on the in-house side

Qualification scrap is real, so budget film and press time for it instead of discovering it in month two.

If the totals land within a few percent of each other, the honest answer is not yet. Bring printing in-house when the gap is decisive and when the non-cost benefit, days rather than weeks from approved artwork to sellable pouch, justifies the operational load. For a broader view of the economics, see Arrow’s article on the real cost savings of in-house short-run digital printing.

Readiness Checklist: What to Have in Place Before You Commit Capital

In-house pouch printing fails on process discipline more often than on equipment, so any unchecked item below is a fix-first item.

Work through these nine prerequisites honestly. Anything unchecked is a fix-first item, not a launch item.

  1. Artwork version control with approval gates. One system of record, locked versions, and a named approver for regulatory fields. No press should be able to run an unapproved file.
  2. A named owner for color management. Press profiles, brand color targets, and proofing standards need one accountable person, not a committee.
  3. A substrate qualification plan with your film supplier. Which structures, in what order, against what acceptance criteria, agreed before installation.
  4. A defined converting path. Pouch making in-house, at a pouch maker, or rollstock direct to your form-fill-seal line. Decide now, because it changes your layout and slitting plan.
  5. Space, utilities, and material handling. Roll weights, unwind clearance, power, climate control, and a home for qualified film inventory.
  6. Trained operator coverage across shifts. One trained operator is a single point of failure during a seasonal build.
  7. A QA method for seal and barrier verification. Seal strength, leak, and print-durability checks with documented pass/fail criteria.
  8. A pilot SKU set with success criteria. Two or three high-churn or seasonal SKUs on one structure, with targets for quality, changeover time, and cost per pouch.
  9. Schedule integration. Connect print jobs to production planning through your ERP or scheduling system so film prints against the build schedule. This step turns shorter lead times into real inventory reduction.

One caveat no equipment decision removes: substrate suitability, migration, food-contact status, and labeling content must be validated with your film supplier, your co-manufacturer, and qualified regulatory counsel against FDA food-contact and US labeling requirements. Equipment capability and regulatory compliance are separate questions, and they need separate owners. Arrow Systems sells printing hardware and does not provide regulatory or compliance advisory services.

ArrowJet Aqua 800M: Where a Wide-Web Water-Based Inkjet Printer Fits

The ArrowJet Aqua 800M is Arrow Systems’ wide-web water-based inkjet printer for digital flexible packaging printed in-house.

Arrow Systems is an industrial label and flexible packaging printing equipment supplier. The Aqua 800M is a water-based inkjet printer built for brands and co-manufacturers that want flexible packaging printing on the plant floor rather than in a converter’s queue.

The workflow it is built around

The buyer profile it suits

High-mix confectionery portfolios with short-to-medium runs, frequent artwork revisions, private-label and club-pack variants of one base product, seasonal SKU waves, and flavor tests that never justified a plate set.

The profile that should not buy it

A small number of long-running core SKUs on one or two stable structures with little artwork churn. That portfolio is better served by a converter relationship, and Arrow would rather say so early than sell against the math.

Frequently Asked Questions — In-House Flexible Packaging Printing

Common questions from confectionery packaging, operations, and procurement teams weighing in-house flexible packaging printing.

Do we need to make pouches in-house too, or just print the film?

Printing and pouch making are separable, and most brands do not start with both. A common path is to print rollstock in-house, then send it to a pouch maker for stand-up pouches and gusseted pouches, or feed it directly to a vertical form-fill-seal or flow-wrap line for bars and family bags. That keeps capital and learning curve focused on print and lamination while converting stays with a partner who already holds the tooling. Decide your converting path before installation, because it sets slitting specs, roll sizes, and floor layout.

How many candy SKUs do we need before in-house flexible packaging printing makes sense?

There is no universal threshold, and any vendor who quotes one is guessing. What matters is the ratio of SKU count and revision frequency to run length per order. Dozens of active SKUs with short reorders, several film structures, seasonal waves, and regular artwork changes build a strong case. A dozen SKUs on long, stable runs and one structure usually does not, regardless of total footage. Run the landed-cost table above against your own converter invoices and overage history before you set a number.

How does digital printing on flexible packaging differ from flexographic and rotogravure?

Flexographic and rotogravure presses transfer ink from plates or engraved cylinders, so every artwork revision needs new tooling and setup, and they are most efficient on long runs of a single design. Digital inkjet printing applies the image directly from a file, so an artwork change needs no plates or cylinders, which suits many SKUs, seasonal graphics, and short reorders. Conventional presses generally keep the advantage on long, stable runs. Film structure, surface treatment, lamination, and seal testing still apply to both, so qualify your films either way.

Can in-house digital flexible packaging printing handle the barrier films our gummies and chocolate require?

Barrier performance comes from the film structure and lamination, not from the printing method. The real question is whether a given press prints reliably on the structures you have already qualified. That depends on surface treatment, topcoat, ink chemistry, and how the printed web behaves through lamination, forming, and sealing. On the ArrowJet Aqua 800M, film substrates require offline pre-treatment, so surface preparation belongs in your qualification plan. Test on your actual candidate films rather than assuming, and take food-contact, migration, and labeling questions to your film supplier, co-manufacturer, and regulatory counsel before any production commitment.

When should a confectionery brand keep outsourcing flexible packaging print?

Keep outsourcing when a handful of core SKUs run long, stable orders on one or two qualified film structures and the artwork changes only once every few years. In that portfolio a converter will beat you on unit cost and you will not recover the capital. Say that out loud before you build the business case.

What should a landed-cost comparison for confectionery flexible packaging include?

On the outsourced side, include printed film price, plates or cylinders per revision, minimum-order overage never consumed, obsolescence, freight, warehousing, expedite premiums, and the revenue impact of missed seasonal windows. On the in-house side, include equipment and training, consumables, prepress labor, floor space, maintenance, and qualification scrap. If the totals land within a few percent of each other, the honest answer is not yet.

Next Step: Score Your Portfolio Against Five Operational Reads

The go/no-go decision rests on five reads: SKU churn, run length, film structures, obsolescence, and process discipline.

  1. High SKU churn. Many new, seasonal, or retailer-specific SKUs arrive each year.
  2. Short run lengths per order. Each purchase order covers hundreds to low thousands of pouches.
  3. Several active film structures. Each structure carries its own qualification work and minimum order.
  4. Heavy obsolescence and minimum-order overage. Stranded film is a recurring line in your ledger.
  5. Process discipline. Version control, color ownership, and seal QA are already in place or ready to be.

Score in-house on most of those and the capital case is real. Score a few long-running core SKUs on stable film and your converter is still the right answer.

Bring your SKU list, run lengths per order, recent converter invoices, minimum-order terms, and current film structures, and Arrow Systems will work through a readiness and landed-cost review with you. If the answer is that you are not ready, Arrow will say so and name what to fix first.

Choose the starting point that fits:

  2. Request a printed sample and pilot-SKU evaluation on your candidate films.

Label Slitting and Matrix Removal: Where Converters Lose Finishing Time

Label slitting and matrix removal, plus rewinding, cost converters more finishing time than the die through stops, rethreads, and rejected rolls.

Most lost finishing time on a label converting line comes from the three steps after the die: matrix removal (breaks and tears), slitting (lane drift and edge defects), and rewinding (rolls that do not match the customer’s applicator). A finishing line runs only as fast as its slowest step, so a matrix that strips cleanly at half the die’s speed holds the whole line to half speed. The fixes start upstream with minimum bridge widths, stored setup settings, and confirmed roll specs. Running laminate, die-cut, strip, slit, and rewind as one pass removes intermediate handling and threading waste. Arrow Systems builds that single pass three ways: the Arrow EZCut 350R with digital blade cutting, the Aries with semi-rotary die cutting, and the ArrowCut Nova 330R with die-free laser cutting.

Key Takeaways

  • A finishing line runs only as fast as its slowest step, and when downtime codes lump stripping, slitting, and rewinding together, the real bottleneck stays hidden.
  • Most label matrix removal problems trace to label geometry (narrow bridges, nested shapes, tight gaps), material behavior (adhesive bleed, liner release), or mechanics (strip angle, take-up tension, speed ramp).
  • A slitting job typically needs one more blade than it has lanes when both edges are trimmed, and setup time grows with every lane change.
  • A finished roll that misses the applicator’s core size, outside diameter, wind direction, or labels-per-roll count is a rejected roll, regardless of print quality.
  • Rated speed is not running speed: the Arrow EZCut 350R slits at up to 100 m/min but die-cuts at up to 9 m/min, and the ArrowCut Nova 330R produces about 10,800 labels per hour on 100 mm circles versus about 6,060 on 100 mm squares.

Why Do Slitting, Stripping, and Rewinding Get Blamed Less Than the Die?

Die-cutting is easy to inspect and measure, while matrix, slit, and rewind faults get logged under other causes, so they rarely get fixed.

Die-cutting is easy to evaluate. The tooling can be inspected, the cut depth can be measured, and the result is either clean or it isn’t.

The steps after the die are harder to read. Operators often log a matrix break as a “die issue,” a wandering slit as press registration, and a telescoped roll as a shipping complaint. When downtime codes don’t separate stripping, slitting, and rewinding, the real cause stays hidden.

That matters because a finishing line runs only as fast as its slowest step. If the matrix strips cleanly at only half the die’s capable speed, the whole line runs at half speed. That single step becomes the finishing line throughput bottleneck, whatever the die is rated for.

What each post-die finishing step does

Matrix removal (stripping)
Matrix removal peels the waste face stock left between die-cut labels off the liner and winds it onto a take-up spindle, leaving finished labels on the liner.
Label slitting
Label slitting cuts the stripped web lengthwise into individual lanes, each one becoming a finished roll of the width the customer specified.
Rewinding
Rewinding winds each slit lane onto a core at a controlled tension, to the outside diameter, wind direction, and label count the customer’s applicator requires.

Matrix Removal: Where Breaks, Tears, and Stops Actually Come From

Label matrix removal problems trace to three sources: label geometry, material behavior, and strip mechanics at speed.

Common causes of matrix breaks

Geometry
Thin matrix bridges, small or nested shapes, tight gaps, and round corners create weak points in the waste web that tear under take-up tension.
Materials
Adhesive bleed can re-bond the matrix to label edges. Face stock stiffness and liner release level change how easily the waste lifts away from the liner.
Mechanics
Strip angle, take-up tension, and speed ramp determine whether the matrix peels away cleanly or tears.

Reducing matrix stripping waste at prepress and setup

The cheapest fix often comes before the job reaches finishing. A slightly wider gap between labels can strengthen the matrix enough to strip faster. Agree on minimum bridge widths by material family with your die supplier, then build them into prepress templates.

At setup, record the strip angle, tension, and ramp that worked for each shape and material. Starting from known-good settings typically reduces both threading waste and matrix stripping waste.

Slitting: Blade Count, Web Width, and Speed Limits

Blade count, web width, and minimum lane width set what one slitting pass can do; label slitting speed depends on the rest of the line.

Blade count vs. lane count
A job typically needs one more blade than it has lanes when both edges are trimmed. The machine’s maximum blade count, web width range, and minimum lane width set the limits of a single pass.
Slitting blade setup
Razor slitting is quick to set and suits many films and papers. Rotary or shear slitting typically gives cleaner edges on tougher materials but needs more careful positioning. With either method, setup time grows with lane changes, because every moved blade means measuring, locking, and test-running.
Edge quality and dust
Dull blades or incorrect blade engagement can leave ragged edges and paper dust. That debris can contaminate adhesive and interfere with downstream sensors.
Label web guide accuracy
Web guide accuracy determines whether slits stay in the gap between labels. Web wander shows up as inconsistent lane widths or slits that nick the labels.
Label slitting speed
Rated slitting speed is a ceiling. Practical speed depends on the material, lane count, blade type, and whether die-cutting, stripping, and rewinding can keep pace in the same pass.

Rewinding: Tension, Core Size, and Roll Diameter for the Applicator

Rewinding finished label rolls is the step the customer handles; if a roll won’t load on the applicator, the job has failed.

Rewinding is the step your customer actually handles. If a roll won’t load on the customer’s applicator, the job has failed regardless of print quality.

Roll rewind tension
Rolls wound too loosely can telescope or shift in transit. Rolls wound too tightly can squeeze out adhesive or cause labels to flag, especially stiff films near the core. Tension often needs to taper as the roll builds.
Core size
Common label cores are 1-inch and 3-inch, but customers may specify others. Confirm the core size before the run starts.
Finished roll diameter and labels per roll
The applicator sets the maximum finished roll diameter, and the customer’s line often sets the labels-per-roll count. An oversized finished roll usually means a rejected roll.
Wind direction
The wind (labels in or out) and the unwind position (which edge leads) must match how the customer’s applicator feeds.
Counting and splices
Accurate counts support the labels-per-roll spec and billing. Flag splices and handle them according to the customer’s tolerance, because some applicators handle splices poorly.

How Do Die-Cutting, Stripping, Slitting, and Rewinding Work in One Pass?

A single pass runs laminate, die-cut, strip, slit, and rewind on one web path, removing intermediate rolls and their threading waste.

Single-pass workflow: laminate (if needed), die-cut, strip, slit, rewind

  1. Laminate the printed web for protection, if the job requires it.
  2. Die-cut labels in register with the print.
  3. Strip the waste matrix to take-up.
  4. Slit the web into finished lanes.
  5. Rewind the lanes to the specified core, outside diameter, and wind direction.

What changes in a single pass

Fewer handling steps
There are no intermediate rolls to stage, move, and rethread between finishing operations.
One registration reference
Die and slit positions share a single web path, which limits drift between passes.
Less threading waste
Every offline pass adds its own lead-in and lead-out waste, so removing passes removes that waste.
Stored job settings
Saving lane positions, tensions, and speeds by job family makes setups more repeatable.

Trade-offs of single-pass finishing

Line speed is set by the slowest step, so a difficult matrix still caps the whole pass. Operator skill still matters for threading, strip setup, and tension judgment. Some specialty or long-run jobs may still fit better offline.

Which Inline Finishing Configuration Fits Your Job Mix: Arrow EZCut 350R, Aries, or ArrowCut Nova 330R?

The right configuration depends on which step limits you today and how you cut: digital blades, semi-rotary dies, or a die-free laser.

Arrow Systems, a manufacturer of digital label presses and label finishing systems, offers three ways to run laminate, cut, strip, and slit as one pass. The main difference is the cutting method, because it decides tooling cost, changeover time, and which step sets your line speed.

Arrow EZCut 350R: digital blade cutting with high-speed rotary slitting
The Arrow EZCut 350R is a roll-to-roll digital die cutter that laminates, cuts, removes matrix, slits, and sheets labels in one machine. Its cutting heads (4 standard, up to 6) adjust their spacing automatically, so there is no physical die to order. Round-knife rotary slitting runs at up to 100 m/min with 5 slitting knives as standard, expandable to 15, across slitting widths of 10 to 330 mm. An ultrasonic web guide keeps feeding straight, and a CCD camera reads printed code marks to change jobs automatically. It suits short, on-demand runs with multi-lane, slitting-heavy layouts.
Aries: semi-rotary die cutting for repeat shapes at volume
The Aries is a semi-rotary label finishing machine that laminates, die-cuts, removes matrix, and slits in one pass at up to 30 m/min. Step 1: Confirm your typical and maximum lane countsLane count decides how many slitting knives you need. Jobs that regularly exceed five lanes point toward a finisher with higher slitting capacity.

Step 3: Count the jobs that need laminationIf a large share of work needs lamination, keep it inside the same pass rather than adding an offline step with its own threading waste.

Frequently Asked Questions: Label Slitting, Matrix Removal, and Rewinding

Common questions from converter operations, production, and finishing leads about stripping, slitting, and rewinding label rolls.

What causes the label matrix to break during stripping?
Matrix breaks usually come from narrow bridges between labels, small or nested shapes, tight gaps, and round corners that weaken the waste web. Adhesive bleed, face stock stiffness, and liner release add to the risk. Strip angle, take-up tension, and aggressive speed ramps are the most common setup causes to check first.
How many slitting blades do I need for a label job?
Most jobs need one more blade than the number of lanes when both edges are trimmed, and fewer when no edge trim is taken. Your slitter’s maximum blade count, minimum lane width, and web width limits determine whether a job runs in one pass. Standardize blade layouts by job family to shorten setup.
What rewind tension and roll diameter should finished label rolls have?

There is no universal setting. Tension should be firm enough to prevent telescoping but not so tight that adhesive oozes or labels flag, and it often tapers as the roll builds. Finished roll diameter, core size, wind direction, and labels per roll should match the end user’s applicator specification, confirmed before production.

Is inline label finishing faster than running separate finishing passes?
Often, but not always. A single pass removes intermediate handling, rethreading, and extra lead-in waste, which typically matters most on short runs with frequent changeovers. However, line speed is limited by the slowest step, so a difficult matrix or high lane count can still cap throughput. Results depend on material and job mix.

Next Steps: Find Your Finishing Constraint

Audit finishing stops by step for two weeks before changing equipment; the pattern usually points to one dominant constraint.

  • Code downtime separately for matrix removal, slitting, and rewinding so the real cause is visible.
  • Set minimum bridge widths by material family and build them into prepress templates.
  • Store known-good strip, tension, and lane settings by job family to shorten setups.
  • Confirm core, outside diameter, wind direction, and labels per roll against the customer’s applicator before every run.
Before changing equipment or blaming the die, audit your finishing stops by step for two weeks. Log every stop, rethread, and rejected roll as matrix removal, slitting, or rewinding, and note the material and shape involved. The pattern usually points to one dominant constraint. That tells you whether setup standards, prepress changes, or a consolidated pass is the right next move.

Limited Edition Spirits Label Printing: 4 Holiday Delay Fixes

Limited edition spirits label printing runs late because of the calendar, not the press: four sequential waits push labels past the bottling slot.

Limited-edition holiday spirits and wine labels usually miss their bottling date because four waits run one after another: physical proof rounds, minimum order quantity (MOQ) commitments, premium finishing queues, and cutting dies ordered only after artwork is final. Each wait has a fix. Name one approver and settle TTB COLA questions before the first proof round, size orders to the bottle count plus a defined overage, lock the embellishment spec before proofing, and fix the dieline geometry before design begins or remove the die altogether. Teams that bring proofing, printing, and finishing in-house with equipment such as the ArrowJet Aqua 330R II, ArrowJet UV 330H, and ArrowCut Nova 330R run these steps in parallel against their own bottling calendar.

Key Takeaways

  • Proofing: Holiday label delays start with proof loops, so name one final approver, use one proof checklist, and settle TTB COLA questions before round one.
  • Quantity: Order limited release bottle labels to the actual bottle count plus a defined overage, not to a plate-based converter minimum.
  • Finishing: Lock the white ink, varnish, and metallic spec before proofing starts, and test it on real stock, including ice-bucket and condensation exposure.
  • Cutting: Fix the dieline geometry before creative begins, order any steel die while proofing is underway, or remove the die dependency with laser finishing.
  • In-house equipment: The ArrowJet Aqua 330R II prints short-run roll labels, the ArrowJet UV 330H adds white ink and varnish effects, and the ArrowCut Nova 330R cuts shapes without a steel die.

Why Do Seasonal Spirits Releases Miss the Q4 Window?

Holiday spirits releases run against fixed bottling, retail, and gift-packaging dates, and labels are usually the last variable item on that path.

This guide is for distillery and winery packaging, operations, and compliance leads planning a Q4 release. Holiday releases run against three dates the packaging team does not control.

Bottling or co-packer slot

Bottling and co-packer slots are booked months ahead and often have little room to move once confirmed.

Distributor and retailer holiday sets

Distributor and retailer holiday sets close on schedule, whether or not the seasonal SKU has arrived.

Gift-box and gift-tube deliveries

Gift boxes and gift tubes must match the final label dimensions and placement, so every label change has to be checked against secondary packaging.

Glass, closures, and liquid are committed early, while artwork is often the final creative decision. Gift season bottle labeling adds coordination with secondary packaging, which raises the stakes on every late label change.

Limited release bottle labels are especially exposed. Quantities are small, finishes are premium, creative approval comes late, and bottle shapes and neck labels are often unique to the release. Conventional converter workflows handle that combination more slowly than almost any other job type.

An Illustrative Q4 Release Scenario

In an illustrative scenario, a craft distillery plans about 3,000 numbered cask-strength bottles. Artwork is final in late August, the mobile bottler is booked for mid-October, and gift tubes are on order. Six weeks later, everything is ready except the labels.

The Four Label Lead-Time Waits at a Glance

Four sequential waits push limited-edition labels past the bottling slot, and each one has its own timeline position and its own fix.

Diagnosis 1: Outsourced Proofing and Revision Cycles

Physical proof rounds add transit and review time, so a few days per round can grow into weeks before production can start.

Proofing delay symptom

Approval drags on. Each proof round brings a new comment, and the run date keeps moving.

Proofing delay root cause

Color and finish can only be judged on real stock. A PDF will not show how a deep burgundy prints on embossed or textured estate paper, or how ink sits on clear or metallic film. Proofs therefore ship physically, and a label proof approval delay of a few 

days per round can grow into weeks across three rounds.

Proofing timeline position

Proofing sits directly after artwork release, before anything else can start. Every day lost in proofing pushes back every downstream step.

Proofing fix this season

  • Name one final approver and one backup.
  • Use a proof checklist that covers color, legal copy, bottle numbering, and finish placement.
  • Treat TTB COLA label timing as a proof-stage question. Some label changes require a new or revised Certificate of Label Approval (COLA) from the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB), while others are allowable revisions that need no new COLA.

TTB allowable revisions

TTB lists the changes permitted on an approved label without a new COLA on pages 3 and 4 of TTB Form 5100.31. According to TTB’s allowable revisions guidance, examples include changing label shape, background color, or font colors and adding a vintage date. Check the current form or ask your compliance advisor before late edits, so COLA timing does not surprise you in round three.

Diagnosis 2: Minimum Order Quantities Forcing Early Commitment

Plate-based minimum order quantities force overbuying on small releases and pull the artwork lock earlier than marketing needs.

MOQ symptom

The team orders far more labels than it has bottles, and the converter wants final art before the team is ready.

MOQ root cause

Plate-based converter workflows are built around minimum order quantities (MOQs). A release of a few hundred or a few thousand bottles often falls below those minimums, which forces overbuying. Securing a production slot also forces an early artwork lock.

MOQ timeline position

MOQ scheduling sits at the very front of the calendar. It pulls the art lock earlier and shrinks marketing’s creative window, and late changes still happen anyway.

MOQ fix this season

  • Size orders to the actual bottle count plus a defined overage for setup, application waste, and spoilage.
  • Ask converters whether a digital short run avoids plate minimums.
  • Flag vintage- or year-specific elements, such as dates, bottle numbers, and release names, because those labels become scrap once the season ends.

For short run spirits labels, the goal is to print what the release needs, not what a press minimum dictates.

Diagnosis 3: Premium Finishing Adding Days

White underprint, spot varnish, and foil-look accents can each add a pass or a handoff, and every finishing station has its own queue.

Premium finishing symptom

The labels are printed but sit waiting for embellishment.

Premium finishing root cause

Gift-season buyers expect strong shelf presence, which often means foil-look accents, white underprint on clear or metallic stock, and spot varnish. Each effect can require an extra pass or a handoff to another station. Premium spirits label finishing is where converter schedules quietly stretch.

Premium finishing timeline position

Embellishment sits between print and cut, often behind other customers’ jobs.

Premium finishing fix this season

  • Finalize the embellishment spec before proofing starts, not during it, including white ink coverage, varnish zones, and metallic areas.
  • Test on the actual substrate, because a metallic spirits label behaves differently from a textured wine paper.
  • Validate durability for ice-bucket and condensation exposure, especially for sparkling wine and chilled spirits, by confirming scuff resistance, wet rub, and adhesive performance on cold, wet glass before release.

Diagnosis 4: Cutting Dies Ordered After Artwork Is Final

Custom steel dies for shaped fronts and neck labels carry their own lead time, which often starts only after artwork is approved.

Cutting die symptom

Artwork is approved, and then the converter reports that the cutting die has its own lead time.

Cutting die root cause

Unique bottle shapes, shaped fronts, neck labels, closure strips, and numbered collector labels often need custom steel dies. Many teams do not order the die until artwork is locked, so die lead time runs after approval instead of alongside it.

Cutting die timeline position

Die lead time sits after approval and right before cutting, adding a separate wait to the critical path.

Cutting die fix this season

  • Lock the dieline geometry before creative begins, and treat it as a fixed constraint for designers.
  • Order the die as soon as the geometry is confirmed, while proofing is still underway.
  • Check label dimensions against gift-box or gift-tube windows at the same time.
  • Remove the die dependency entirely with digital die-free finishing, which cuts shapes directly from a digital file.
